Equipment

Full setup preset

A full setup saves the rifle, the bullet and the sight as they stand right now, in one entry, and loading it replaces all three.

Presets you save are sent to a list everyone using this page can see and load, and anyone can add to it. Do not put anything in a preset name you would not publish. You can delete the ones this browser saved; you cannot delete other people's.

Zeroing conditions

Your zero was set on one particular day. Turn this on and the scope angle is solved under those conditions while the bullet flies through today's air — which is what actually happens. Leave it off and the solver assumes you zeroed in the conditions you are shooting in now.

Environment

Where you are

Both of these leave the device. “Use my location” asks the browser for your coordinates; “Fetch live weather” sends those coordinates to the Open-Meteo public API and fills in temperature, pressure, humidity and wind. Nothing else on this page ever contacts the network, and neither runs unless you press it.

Atmosphere

Station pressure is what a Kestrel reads — not the altimeter setting corrected to sea level. Positive shot angle is uphill. Latitude and azimuth drive the Coriolis term.

Wind

90° 3 o'clock

Drag the dial, or use the arrow keys. The clock is relative to your shot: 12 o'clock blows from the target into your face, 3 o'clock from your right.

Output

A turret factor other than 1.000 scales the clicks you dial. Set it only if you have measured your scope's tracking on a tall target: a scope that moves 9.7 MIL when you dial 10.0 has a factor of 10.0 / 9.7 = 1.031.

Shot log

Every logged shot stores the prediction, what you actually dialled, where it landed, and the complete setup that produced it — bullet, rifle, zero, atmosphere and wind. It is recorded to check whether the model is realistic; it never feeds back into the solver, because a prediction corrected by the last observation is no longer an independent test of anything.

Reset

Ported from the PyBallisticsV2 solver (Python + NumPy), validated cell-by-cell against it across 22 configurations. The canonical M852 case reproduces −1357.3097 cm of drop at 1000 m. Aerodynamic coefficients: BRL MR-3733 (McCoy); standard drag functions G7/G1 per McCoy. Weather by Open-Meteo. Academic tool — verify against your own data before trusting a solution.
